#7413. AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”

As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly.

“Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

Using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also shows that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily users and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Google's core updates arrive with a start time and a scope. Everything else you've read about them came from somewhere else.

The routine is familiar by now. Google posts a sentence. It has a name, a start time, and a note that the rollout may take up to two weeks. Within the hour, somebody has published a “what we know so far.” By the evening, there’s a list of winners and losers. Before the week is out, with the rollout still running, there’s a recovery guide in seven steps.

I’ve watched this for most of 20 years. The only part that has changed is the sentence. It used to be longer.

When Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it. The post said what the change was for: sites that add little, copy from others, or just aren’t very useful. It said how big it was: 11.8% of queries. You could argue with the result, and plenty did, but there was a stated target to argue with.

Here is the entry for the November 2026 core update, which started on Nov. 10. It was released. It applies globally and in all languages. It may take up to two weeks. That’s the lot: three facts, none of them about your site.

Google has been open about why. In a Q&A on Search updates, it said it changes Search thousands of times a year and announces the ones it considers notable, about 10 a year when it last counted in public. Its core updates documentation adds that smaller core updates go out continually and aren’t announced at all. So a named update is a ranking change that Google decided to put on a calendar. The calendar entry tells you when. It tells you nothing about what changed, or about what happens in between.

The announcement shrank to a timestamp, and the commentary expanded to fill the space.

The date does have a use. Google’s own guidance uses it: wait a week after the rollout finishes, then compare that week with the week before it started. The date draws a line through your data so you know where to look. Visibility trackers do a similar job across the market; they show which sites moved.

What neither of them shows is why. Which system changed, and why it moved your site in particular, is known inside Google and nowhere else. A rank tracker and a strong feeling won’t close that gap.

That hasn’t slowed anyone down. An obscure tool vendor published a winners-and-losers study of the November update within a day or two of the launch. It gave the wrong start date and called it the sixth core update of the year. Google’s dashboard lists three. I’d say the analysis was rushed, but that implies there was something to analyze.

The closest thing I know to a core update is the annual performance review.

Anyone who has had a job knows the meeting. You walk in and get a rating that was settled long before the meeting was booked. It reflects the year you had. It also reflects the people you were measured against, because plenty of companies calibrate ratings across a team; you can do the same work as last year and drop a grade because three colleagues did better. Search works the same way. A page is ranked against every other page that could answer the query, so a site can lose ground without changing anything.

A core update is review day. It’s when the rating becomes visible. Nobody sensible leaves that meeting and asks what changed about the meeting.

The comparison stops in one place. After a review you get a manager, written feedback and a chance to ask what went wrong. After a core update you get a dashboard entry. That missing conversation is the entire market for update commentary: an industry of people offering to be the manager who explains your rating, none of whom were in the calibration room.

The strongest objection to all this is that the losses are real, and it’s correct. Companies do lose a large share of their organic revenue overnight, and people lose jobs over it. The practitioners who spend their time on recoveries are dealing with real businesses in real trouble.

There’s also evidence that sometimes the reviewer gets it wrong. In October 2024, Google invited a group of independent publishers hit by the September 2023 helpful content update to its campus. According to people who were in the room, they were told their content wasn’t the problem, and that they shouldn’t count on getting their traffic back. That is an awkward fact for anyone, me included, who says most affected sites had it coming.

Look at what it does to the recovery guide, though. If the content wasn’t the issue, “seven steps for improving your content” were never going to work. The publishers with the best case against Google are also the best evidence that nobody outside it could diagnose them.

Now the less sympathetic group, which in my experience is the bigger one.

Most of the affected sites I’ve been asked to look at over 20 years had the same history. Somebody decided what they could get away with before finding out what the market already offered. They hadn’t researched what customers needed or looked at how good the existing answers were. They picked keywords with volume, wrote about them, and launched.

When that didn’t work, they went looking for a shortcut, and social media had plenty. A thread with a promise that was too good to be true, and was. A “hack” from somebody who discovered SEO in the summer and by autumn had a conference slot and a YouTube channel. In office terms, that’s career advice from the colleague who joined in August and already runs a workshop. They copied it without asking why it would work. Some of these tricks do work for a few months, which is the worst outcome available, because the fall then lands inside an update window and gets blamed on the update.

Then they hired SEO to make it work, as if rankings were a delivery service for businesses that forgot to have a product. I’ve written about the wall that approach runs into; it hasn’t moved.

This is the employee who did the minimum all year and arrives at the review certain that the rating system has changed, and has brought printouts. In fairness to them, they have a problem that needs solving. “The algorithm changed” is something you can say to a board. “We built a site with nothing to say and then paid someone to get it found” tends not to make the deck.

So there’s a buyer for an outside cause, and the update coverage supplies one. It comes with a diagnosis nobody outside Google could have made and a retainer that renews before the next update can contradict it. The seller gets a client, and the client gets a story. The site stays exactly as useful as it was, which was the problem.

This trade feels legitimate to the people in it because of how the industry thinks about quality.

Take E-E-A-T. Google coined it for its quality raters, and Google’s own documentation says it isn’t a specific ranking factor. The industry read that and sold E-E-A-T audits anyway, with scores for a thing Google says it has no score for. Somewhere there is an author bio that was added to fix a business model.

The traits themselves are older than the initialism. Peter Morville’s user experience honeycomb had “credible,” “useful,” and “valuable” in it in 2004, as facets of a product, with no ranking attached. The industry needed Google to hand it an initialism before it noticed that people prefer things they can trust.

“JavaScript SEO” has the same shape: it’s progressive enhancement, which web developers were practicing before anyone gave it a conference track. I made that case in Stop Learning SEO and won’t repeat it.

If quality is a list of items to tick, then a core update is a new edition of the list, and you need someone to tell you what’s on it. There is never a shortage of volunteers. Back in the office, that’s working to the KPIs. The person who works to the KPIs has to know the moment they change. The person who is good at the job mostly finds out on review day that they still are.

So people who hold quality as a checklist need each update explained; the announcement explains nothing, and so somebody makes one up.

The first question a business could ask after an update is “What did this update change for my site?” Answering it would take the list of systems that changed, how much each one counts, and what every competing page did in the same fortnight. Nobody outside Google has those. You can still pay for an answer. It’ll arrive as a confident PDF with a traffic-light table, and it will tell you to improve content quality, show more expertise, and prune the thin pages.

Now read the PDF from the update before. It says the same thing. So will the one after the next update, because the advice was never derived from the update. If the remedy is the same whatever changed, the change taught nobody anything.

The second question is “what do the people I want as customers need that they can’t already get?” It’s a worse question to be asked. It has no villain and no deadline; it can’t be handed to a thread, and the answer may be that the business has nothing to add yet. It’s also slower and more expensive to answer than a PDF. But it can be answered by people you can find and talk to, and it could have been answered before the site launched.

The fair objection to the second question is Google. Google is in the business of taking in what other people know and serving it back as its own answer, and AI Overviews and AI Mode have made that the main event. The part of the web where people found you through a search result is being eaten, and Google is the one holding the fork. I’ve covered what that did to publishers’ traffic. So why polish anything for a channel that’s shrinking?

Because the second question was never about the channel. A site is a product, and what people need from it doesn’t change when fewer of them arrive through Google. What does change is how much of what you know you should hand over for free. I’ve argued that publishing everything is a terrible business strategy, and I still think so. Holding back the method is sensible. Shipping a site that’s a bare outline of what you’re supposed to be good at is a different decision, and it fails the customer long before it fails a ranking system.

The line between those two is thin, and it’s meant to be. It sits in a different place for every business, and no update, checklist, or thread will tell you where yours is. A search engine certainly won’t; it looks after its own interests, as it always has. The only people who know how much is enough are the ones you’re trying to sell to, which is one more reason to go and ask them.

In the office, it’s the gap between “what did the calibration committee change this year?” and “what did I do this year?” Only one of those is yours to find out, and it’s the one that doesn’t come with somebody else to blame.

Google will post another sentence soon enough. The recovery guide for it already exists. It’s the one from last time.

When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:

As pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and new hybrid work schedules.

On Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some:

#7405. “A government that ‘gets it’”: Canada recommits to federal funding for news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The new budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”

A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”

I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

“We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan said. “They see what Big Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”

RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s big local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a new tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

The labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

“In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said.

There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

“That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”

In the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

But News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

The Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Launched in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results showed the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

“Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”

“Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said.

Some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

Deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

“To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

“When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”

#7402. Google Ads Surcharges Rise To 3% In France And Italy – Local US Advertisers Can Be Billed Too via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Check where your Google Ads run: default location settings can expose local campaigns to France and Italy surcharges rising to 3% on Jan. 1, 2027.

If you manage a Google Ads account, you probably got an email last week saying that ads served in France and Italy will carry a 3% Regulatory Operating Cost starting Jan. 1, 2027. You may have deleted it because you don’t advertise in Europe. Don’t assume you’re off the hook. Google bills these surcharges based on where your ads are actually served, and its default location setting can serve your ads to people who have never set foot in your target area.

I found this out the practical way. I do some pro bono consulting for a retailer on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, and I have access to his Google Ads account. His campaigns are built to reach shoppers within a few miles of his store. On the morning of Nov. 11, his account received two notices from Google Payments, one headed “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in Italy” and the other “Surcharge Updates for Ads Served in France.”

I scanned them and moved on. Then I went back, because I suspected plenty of Search Engine Journal readers were asking the same question I was. Why is a neighborhood retailer in New York getting billing notices about two countries he isn’t targeting?

The short answer is that the emails are a warning, not a bill. Whether they become a bill depends on settings most local advertisers have never opened.

Google calls these charges jurisdiction-specific surcharges. Some are labeled Digital Services Tax (DST) fees and some are labeled Regulatory Operating Costs, but they work the same way. They are added to your invoice on top of your ad spend, and on top of any account budget you set.

Here is how the rates for Google Ads stand on Google’s help page, before and after Jan. 1, 2027.

Two former entries are off the list. Google says ads served in India stopped carrying a 2% charge on Sept. 1, 2024, and ads served in Canada no longer carry the 2.5% DST fee.

The same increases apply to Display & Video 360, and Google’s help page says YouTube placements bought on a reservation basis carry the surcharges too.

In Italy, the jump is half a point. In France, it is a full point, which means the fee itself rises by 50%. Turkey moves the other way.

See also: Ask A PPC: How Will The Tariffs Impact My PPC Campaigns?

Google’s help page states the rule plainly. The charge applies every time an ad is served in one of these jurisdictions, “regardless of where your actual business is located.” The surcharge is calculated on the impressions or clicks served in each country, so an account that serves nothing in France pays nothing in France.

That would seem to settle it for my client. But a few paragraphs further down, Google adds a warning that you might show ads to users in a country you never targeted “because your business is in a location of interest for them.” Google also says it is the advertiser’s responsibility to make sure campaign target settings are correct, and that it will not refund surcharges triggered by legitimate clicks and impressions served according to those settings.

In plain English, if your settings let a shopper in Milan see your ad, you pay the Italy surcharge on that impression, and you don’t get it back.

See also: 13 Google Ads Settings To Check When Running International PPC Campaigns

Google’s advanced location options give you two choices for who counts as being in your target area. “Presence or interest” reaches people who are in, regularly in, or who’ve shown interest in your targeted locations. “Presence” reaches only people who are in or regularly in them.

Presence or interest is the default, and Google labels it as recommended. Google supports that recommendation with its own data, saying advertisers in travel, real estate, and education who switched to it saw 5% more conversions on Search campaigns. That is Google’s claim from Google’s internal data, and it covers three verticals, not retail.

For a store on Madison Avenue, “interest” is where Europe gets in. Someone in Paris searching for shops on the Upper East Side has shown interest in New York. Under the default, your ad can serve to that person, and the impression lands in France.

The controls have also been widening. Demand Gen campaigns picked up the same Presence or interest versus Presence choice in late 2025, and AI Max for Search has added options for reaching people based on locations of interest. More automation in where ads go means more chances to serve impressions in places you didn’t pick.

Giovanni Perilli, a funnel marketing consultant who writes about European ad costs, published a breakdown the same day the emails went out. The France email he received did not mention Italy at all. In his words, the email “leaves out the change that matters most to anyone advertising in Italy.”

That matches my own experience, with a twist. My client’s account got two separate emails, one per country. Advertisers who received only one should check the help page rather than assume nothing else changed.

Perilli also turns the surcharge into numbers a PPC manager can use. Because the fee is added on top of what you spend, he multiplies a cost-per-acquisition by 1.03 and divides a return on ad spend by 1.03. A €40 CPA effectively becomes €41.20. A ROAS of four becomes about 3.88. If your break-even ROAS is 2.5, your real target in France and Italy is now about 2.58.

Those are small numbers. On thin retail margins in the first quarter, they are not nothing.

See also: Google Says Changing tCPA & Budgets Won’t Reset Learning – 6 BFCM Takeaways

Google’s help page says the France and Italy charges cover part of the cost of complying with digital services tax legislation in those countries. The tax news over the past year lines up with that.

French lawmakers voted in October 2025 to double France’s digital services tax from 3% to 6% for the largest platforms, but the budget bill carrying it was rejected a month later, and the rate remains 3%. Italy’s DST has applied at a 3% rate since 2020, and its 2025 budget law removed the domestic revenue threshold that had kept some companies out of scope. Turkey went the other direction, cutting its DST from 7.5% to 5% this year and to 2.5% on Jan. 1, 2027. Google’s Turkey surcharge falls to 2.25% on the same date

Google also has company now. Meta began charging its own location fees on July 1, 2026, at 3% in France, Italy, and Spain, as Bloomberg reported. From January, Google and Meta charge the same 3% in all three countries.

Here’s my read. Digital services taxes were sold to voters as a way to make big tech pay. The platforms are now itemizing those taxes on advertisers’ invoices, and some of those advertisers are small businesses on another continent. Whatever you think of the policy, the bill has moved down the chain, and PPC managers are the ones who have to explain it to clients.

Here are four steps I’m taking in my client’s account, and I’d suggest you take them in yours.

I almost ignored these notices, and I’ve been reading Google Ads billing emails since 2003. My advice is to treat them as an audit prompt, not as spam. The surcharge itself is modest. The real story is how many local accounts may be serving ads in Europe without anyone deciding they should.

My client’s ads are meant for the Upper East Side, not Paris or Milan. I’d rather confirm that in a report before Jan. 1 than discover it on a February invoice.

#7401. With event costs up and funding down, journalism organizations cancel conferences and cut staff

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”

RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

At the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

“Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”

LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”

“Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said.

OpenNews said in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”

The future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”

The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩]

The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year.

And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me.

But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. #7397. Indonesia’s new copyright bill would force Google and Meta to pay to aggregate news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

On Wednesday, Meta, TikTok, and Google testified in the Indonesian parliament in opposition to a new copyright bill. The proposed law would require digital platforms to pay news publishers in Indonesia for aggregating and previewing their content, according to a new report from Reuters.

RELATED ARTICLEThis citizen-run organization is teaching thousands of Indonesians to fact-checkHanaa' TameezApril 12, 2023The bill does not distinguish between aggregation and republication. Tech platforms would have to pay even when they surface news link previews or story snippets in their products, including AI search products. The law would also force platforms to compensate publishers when their journalism is used to train AI models.

Any compensation would be paid through a state-run management organization, which would then distribute the funds to publishers. Platforms that don’t comply could face sanctions, including the loss of their local business permits.

If the bill does pass, Indonesia would become the first country in Southeast Asia to formally fold AI into its copyright law.

Social media and search engine companies have come out in force against the bill, with Google leading the campaign.

Indonesia is a massive market for global digital platforms with roughly 230 million internet users. In 2023, Indonesia had the fifth-most Google users of any country in the world, with traffic reaching 4.42 billion searches.

RELATED ARTICLEMeta will remove legit news from Facebook and Instagram in Canada — but may leave the bad stuff upLaura Hazard OwenAugust 2, 2023As of October 2026, 92% of internet users in Indonesia reported using WhatsApp, with Instagram and Facebook falling close behind at 84% and 79% respectively, according to We Are Social’s Digital 2027 report.

On Wednesday, a Google official argued that the bill would limit access to news, according to Reuters.

Berni Moestafa, Meta’s head of public policy in Indonesia, testified that if the bill is passed “publishers could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue.”

Back in 2023, Canada passed the Online News Act, its own, albeit narrower law which required platforms like Google and Meta to pay publishers for sharing or linking to their content. Meta responded by blocking news links on Facebook and Instagram in Canada altogether.

#7394. 6.9% Of ChatGPT Conversations Showed Purchase Intent In U.S. Panel via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

U.S. data finds few ChatGPT conversations show intent to buy and most responses name no brand. New insight for teams weighing ChatGPT visibility and ads.

Brands have some insight into how often purchase intent shows up in chat with ChatGPT, based on its presence in 6.9% of conversations in a U.S. opt-in panel analyzed by SparkToro.

Data was provided by Verso, which tracks users’ ChatGPT conversation history when they link their account. The sample size is 41,961 conversations, generated by 12,321 people between Jan. 1 and Oct. 29, 2026. Most of the figures are from a sub-sample which had been statistically weighted to match the demographic characteristics of the U.S. population.

Of ChatGPT’s responses in this sub-sample, 87.9% did not name a single brand, product or business. Based on the analysis, Rand Fishkin (co-founder and CEO of SparkToro) concluded that the primary reason AI visibility matters is Google’s implementation of AI Overviews and AI Mode, rather than ChatGPT itself.

Based upon the purchase-intent graph developed with the weighted group, there are three types of conversation by purpose. In a total of 4.9% of conversations, the person planned to purchase and was continuing to look at the options; another 2.1% were asking questions related to purchasing a specific brand, product or service; while a total of 93.1% showed no intention to purchase.

Fishkin wrote, “I suspect this is bad news for ChatGPT’s advertising opportunities.”

He also referenced SparkToro’s December 2024 analysis of approximately 332 million Google searches. He wrote that 15% or more of searches fit his definition. SparkToro did an analysis of searches done by a U.S. panel via browsers from January 2023 through September 2024. Commercial (a financial, business services or commerce intent) accounted for 14.5% of searches, although the searcher may not have been ready to make a purchase at that time.

Transactional accounted for 0.69%. These categories do not match the categories identified in the ChatGPT graph which measured purchase intentions, so the percentages cannot be compared directly.

In addition to tracking whether people asked about brands, the report also tracked if ChatGPT’s responses named any. In the weighted group, 86.7% of all prompts did not ask for brand, product or company information. Of all prompts, 6.6% asked about several brands, with the remainder being about a single brand (6.7%). On the response side, 7.0% of all responses mentioned multiple brands, products or companies while 5.1% mentioned one; the post’s reported percentage of responses mentioning at least one was 12.1%.

The post’s takeaways describe 12% of ChatGPT usage as part of the buyer journey, though its purchase-intent chart puts conversations with purchase intent at 6.9%.

Images and visual design requests were the top ranked category in the report with a total of 17.6% of conversations. Information and entertainment came second in terms of overall conversations (14.4%), writing and communication third (12.7%), while shopping, brands and local services made up 5.3%.

One category per conversation was assigned, representing the primary goal of each. The output type counts over the topic when someone asks ChatGPT to create something (e.g., if you ask it to write an email asking for a refund from PayPal, that would be categorized as writing instead of shopping).

The percentages shown in the report’s chart vary from the percentages shown in the report’s text by less than two percentage points per category. The percentages provided here reflect the report’s chart.

The panel was also compared to OpenAI’s Signals data for September using the weighted group. OpenAI’s data was heavier towards writing and tech support, while the weighted panel data leaned more toward image requests and how-to questions. The author says the two are fair to compare given that OpenAI almost certainly includes API requests (that Verso does not track) in its numbers.

According to OpenAI’s page, the dataset “reflects only messages within ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, and Pro accounts” and Codex and enterprise usage are excluded from this count; thus excluding API calls as well. In addition, OpenAI presents global message shares whereas the panel shows shares of U.S.-based conversations.

Verso offers a free tool that breaks down a person’s ChatGPT history. Its sign-up terms say Verso stores the imported conversations and includes them, de-identified, in datasets it licenses to research and business customers. According to the post, Verso co-founder Aaron Aknin reached out to the post’s author and supplied the data.

The report also described the panel as skewed toward younger people, women and people at lower income levels. There were 9,675 members in the panel that had demographic information that could be used as a weighting base to match the 2024 United States Census. No usage category varied by more than 1.4 percentage points when the demographics were weighted to these standards.

Before the data analysis was performed, the 131 heaviest users, who generated an average of over 33 prompts per active month, were eliminated. These heavy users accounted for approximately 1% of the total number of panelists, but they were responsible for sending 21% of all prompts. On average each member of the weighted group (excluding the above noted heaviest users) sent 9.9 prompts between January and October.

As most panelists were recorded on mobile phones, the post says this may have caused some of the usage through desktop computers and work accounts to be underreported. API requests are not included in the data set.

Each conversation was coded using a written code book provided to Anthropic’s model called Claude. Each conversation was coded based upon its title, up to six of the user-generated prompts, the initial few lines of ChatGPT’s first few responses and any product cards or bolded names. A second coder independently recoded a random sample of conversations, and the two coders agreed on categories 90% of the time and on brand tags 97% to 99% of the time. The post reports no separate agreement figure regarding its identification of purchase intent.

SparkToro sells audience research software.

For brands splitting AI visibility and ad budgets, the U.S. panel gives a measured share of ChatGPT conversations that involve buying, and it’s under 7%. Fishkin concludes that Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode are what make AI visibility important, and he questions whether tracking ChatGPT visibility is worth it unless Bing rankings and AI visibility are tracked too.

The post explains that the panel reflects what people ask ChatGPT much better than how often they use it. For PPC teams exploring ChatGPT Ads, the 6.9% purchase-intent share offers a snapshot of the conversation mix in a consumer panel with light ChatGPT use, not a count of purchase-related conversations across ChatGPT.

Until panel data includes desktop, work and API use, it’s best to pair purchase-intent figures like this one with your own ChatGPT referral and ad data before adding them to a budget plan. Fishkin also shared that he looks forward to doing more research with Verso.

From new majors to search traffic, newspapers to impeachment: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

It’s been another busy week. Recap it with the second edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. The quiz will appear here through November as a trial run; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

What journalism organization announced this week that it was canceling its annual conference and laying off most of its staff?

“Since we gathered in Chicago for ONA26, many of you have asked when we will be together again,” CEO Niketa Patel wrote. “Unfortunately, it will not be in 2027. ONA has decided to pause our in-person events and will not host a conference in 2027.”

For the first time ever, the press freedom group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) has officially called for the impeachment of a U.S. official. Which one?

“RSF does not take the question of impeachment lightly. In fact, our organization has never before called for the removal of a US official. But the severity and persistence of Carr’s misconduct as FCC chairman demand an extraordinary response. Congress has a constitutional responsibility to hold him accountable. Restoring the FCC’s independence must be central to that effort.”

Emerson College recently announced a new degree program aimed at helping students build “a career across a rapidly changing media landscape.” What’s the program’s name?

“Our new Content Creation major prepares students to be a part of the evolving creator economy, teaching them not only how to produce compelling digital content but also how to build a successful entrepreneurial career.”

What news organization — after a challenging few years — says it is now “within striking distance of break-even,” financially?

“I’ll be honest,” executive editor Matt Murphy said at a conference. “We had years of losses, and steepening losses. That’s the truth. We’re a private company and don’t share the figures, but it was hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars. Now we’re within striking distance of break-even, and I expect next year will be our best year in seven years. We’ve done the right-sizing we needed, which was tough.”

The Echo-Pioneer — the local newspaper in the town of High Level, Alberta (population 4,000) — has an unusual business model. What is it?

Town officials signed a two-year “advertising and readership agreement” in 2025. It’s one of the many ways local Canadian news outlets are trying to stay afloat — most notably the federal Local Journalism Initiative.

Which online publisher’s CEO announced that Google search traffic had “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week” in October?

As a result of the search decline, CEO Steve Huffman announced Reddit would be shifting to a primarily “logged-in experience.”

The Asia-Pacific outlet The Diplomat retracted an interview with a South Korean CEO last week. Why?

“The author presented themselves as a South Korean freelance journalist and claimed to have interviewed Newtype’s CEO. We now know that the journalist fabricated the interview and may not even be who they claimed to be.”

The parliament of an Asian nation is debating requiring tech companies like Google and Meta to pay news outlets when they direct users to their stories. Which nation?

The proposed law would also require compensating news publishers when AI models are trained on news content.

Which international news outlet, sensing a political opening, is expanding its reporting team in the United States?

“Market research indicated there was room to grow among politically liberal Jews in the United States. Gali Arnon, who became the chief executive of Haaretz Group last year, said she wanted the newspaper to become in other countries what it is in Israel: an ‘identity brand.’”

The Cornell Daily Sun saw traffic spike by almost 500% in September.

RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop. For July, August, and September, traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data.

RELATED ARTICLEHow did newspapers in places like Harrisburg, Birmingham, and Syracuse become some of America’s most-read online?Joshua BentonJuly 23, 2025A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com. Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com, Mlive.com, and NJ.com, among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025.

Still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a new website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia. The parent company is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney said.

In Florida, Cape Coral Breeze, a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “Best of Cape Coral” contest, where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website users to our news coverage,” Eckenrode said, and had some success with that strategy.

In September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in New York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump.

On the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. “Our traffic is volatile like everyone else’s, but we had a strong September mainly because a couple of stories performed very well,” said Annika Toernqvist, MediaNews Group’s managing editor for digital for Northern California. Environmental beat reporter Paul Rogers‘ story about a new California law that will ban watering artificial turf “performed exceptionally well on Google and Google Discovery”; 62% of traffic to the story came from search. Stories about the local impact of new state laws consistently do well with the outlet’s readers, according to Toernqvist, and this was “a hot topic with a strong headline.” The story was also the top subscription converter in September. Another story by Rogers covering the proposed renaming of Fremont State Park also drove traffic that month; 86% came from search, mostly from Google Discovery.

Meanwhile, celebrity reporter Martha Ross‘ story about a new book on King Charles’ valet performed well in part thanks to a bump from…the Drudge Report. (“Yes, the Drudge Report still drives traffic,” Toernqvist said; it accounted for 43% of visits to that story.)

#7388. Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems via @sejournal, @martinibuster

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google explains the steps to take to ensure a CDN migration won't backfire and cause a negative impact to SEO.

Googlers Gary Illyes and Cherry Prommawin explain how moving to a CDN can unexpectedly increase crawling and overwhelm the origin server, despite eventually improving website performance. They also share that attempts to control crawler traffic can sometimes accidentally block Googlebot and harm Search visibility.

Illyes and Prommawin explained that moving to a CDN can cause Googlebot to increase crawling because faster server responses signal that the site’s infrastructure can handle more requests. Google’s automated crawling systems interpret the improved performance as an indication that more crawling is possible and responds by gradually increasing the crawl rate.

CDN caches are initially empty and the CDN only starts caching when a browser or bot requests a page at which point the request has to be forwarded to the origin server, where the actual website is at.

When Google increases the crawl rate, the initial crawl is handled by the origin server. But now Googlebot is hitting the server more aggressively and it’s this that can overwhelm the origin server, initially.

“For one, suddenly the crawling metrics suggests the site can handle a larger amount of crawling. And on the flip side, because the CDN caches aren’t yet populated, the origin server still has to serve the requested pages.

Basically, CDNs take the valve off the hose, so now crawlers are drinking from a fire hose.”

“Under normal circumstances, our crawlers operate under an important rule. When a server responds faster, the crawlers assume the infrastructure is healthy and slowly ramp up crawl speed.

…So the crawlers see how fast the server responds, get really excited, and start to crawl the entire site at a higher, higher, and higher speed. But it’s a trap.

People assume a CDN can catch a crawl spike from day one, but …The cache has to be filled up with the assets off the site first.”

Gary Illyes explained that on a first request for a page the CDN has to fetch the page from the origin server first to populate the cache with the content. It’s not until the second request for the page that the cache is populated with the content and begins doing its job.

“…which means your origin server may get slammed by the flood anyway. Now, to be fair, our crawlers take time to ramp up. It won’t happen in a millisecond.

An empty cache means your origin server is still doing all the heavy lifting. Until that cache is populated, your CDN isn’t acting as a shield just yet.”

A CDN cannot serve an un-cached URL without retrieving it first from the origin server and that only happens after a request for that URL is first made. Crawlers visit large numbers of URLs virtually all the time and can generate a substantial amount of origin traffic before the CDN’s caches are fully populated.

This next issue involves accidentally blocking Googlebot and triggering a reduced search presence because Google can no longer crawl and index URLs from a website. Illyes and Prommawin explain it in the context of a website admin flipping a switch at Cloudflare and inadvertently blocking Googlebot.

This is a real problem, I recall an instance in which a popular website’s massive traffic dried up whenever Cloudflare was activated and would return once they turned it off. They had a devil of a time diagnosing why this was happening and the customer service people at the time were unable to help them. It may have been the case, as Illyes and Prommawin noted, that the admin had turned on a strict bot filter that inadvertently blocked Googlebot.

Illyes offered an example of an admin doing exactly that:

“They look at the spiking traffic, assume they are being aggressively scraped by botnets, and naturally, they panic.”

And what sometimes happens next is that an admin might turn on “blanket security rules” that block Googlebot.

“In panic, one might log into their CDN dashboard and turn on the setting to block bots entirely.

…If the CDN detects automated requests, it intercepts them with a CAPTCHA challenge, asking them to click pictures of traffic lights to prove they’re human.

…It sees automated requests, flags it as a bot, and then intercepts with a CAPTCHA. And since our crawlers cannot identify a traffic light, they fail the test.”

What eventually happens with prolonged Googlebot blocking is that Google will begin dropping the pages from the index.

Prommawin suggested that site admins should configure their CDN to allow known and trusted crawlers. This is a method called whitelisting where only crawlers that are on the “allowed” list can get it and all other crawlers cannot.

They also recommend the use of CDN-level rate limiting of Googlebot if the requests on the origin server lead to downtime which can negatively impact legitimate human traffic to the website.

When a site initially starts out with a CDN, the CDN does not have a cache of a website’s content. The cache doesn’t get loaded until it’s requested by a browser or crawler visit.

Cache pre-warming is the process of requesting content from a site so that the content gets loaded onto the CDN. This ensures that the content is already loaded onto the CDN before users request it, which ensures that the content is delivered quickly without the CDN having to first retrieve it from the origin server (the server where the actual content files exist).

Illyes recommends “pre-warming” the cache by programmatically requesting URLs from it so that thE cache is populated in a controlled manner.

“And to survive augmenting your site with a CDN, see if you can pre-warm the caches by programmatically fetching your top URLs through the CDN before you open the floodgates to search engines.”

Google’s main point is that moving to a CDN can create an unexpected combination of faster crawling and increased origin-server demand. That in turn can lead to unintentionally setting aggressive security restrictions that prevent Googlebot from accessing a website.

Three especially important points for SEOs and site owners:

1. Using a CDN can trigger an increase in Googlebot crawling when it detects faster server responses, even though the CDN’s caches have not yet been populated, which in turn means an increase in requests for URLs from the origin server.

2. A CDN migration can inadvertently cause pages to disappear from Google Search due to aggressive security settings intended to stop malicious bots can also lock out Google’s crawlers.

3. Google recommends pre-warming caches, allowing trusted crawlers, and temporarily controlling crawling when server demand becomes excessive.

Read Google’s new CDN documentation here.

#7385. NPR makes fixing its app a key priority in its new strategic plan

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Over the next two years, NPR will address a longstanding listener plea: improving its app.

During a November 12 board of directors meeting, NPR CEO Katherine Maher said the organization will rebuild its digital offerings to be a “service-first, app-first destination” as part of NPR’s 2027-2029 strategic plan, Current reported on Thursday. One goal of the plan is to reach “five million weekly active users on its platforms by 2029” and “to build a monthly engaged digital audience of 40 million.” According to Current, Maher said that the NPR network — which includes more than 200 member radio stations — currently reaches 39 million weekly listeners across broadcast and digital, but the “total potential addressable audience, weekly consumers of news, information and culture who are open to our work, is roughly 153 million Americans. That is nearly four times our current reach.”

In Apple’s App Store, NPR’s app has a 4.7-star rating and more than 78,000 reviews, of which the majority are positive. But reviewers have quibbles.

Bryan Moffett, NPR’s senior vice president of transformation, said NPR+, the broadcaster’s subscription program, brought in $8 million in the 2026 fiscal year, up from $5.5 million in 2025. (NPR+ is available with a donation of $8 a month or more, and offers perks like podcasts without ads.) Maher said new investment in the app will help reach younger audiences and shift NPR’s “median audience age from 60-plus toward 40-plus.”

“We love radio, but we have been so wildly successful there that we’ve largely exhausted its further financial growth,” Maher told the board. “And as it shrinks, we must invert our revenue engine to ensure sustainability across all of our platforms, including radio, but to build a wider funnel through digital offerings, third-party platforms, and new investments in marketing and communication that will tell our story and share our value with the world.”

RELATED ARTICLENPR, the quintessential audio news brand, adapts to a video-first futureSarah ScireSeptember 29, 2026Overhauling the app is just one part of NPR’s strategy to keep up with users’ changing consumption preferences. In September, Sarah Scire reported on the broadcaster leaning into video podcasts with the acquisition of Kevin Roose and Casey Newton’s technology podcast Machine Gods. NPR chief operating officer Ryan Merkley told Current in June that NPR was already working on redesigning the app to better serve member stations and their listeners.

“Fix the app,” departing public editor Kelly McBride told NPR leaders during the meeting. “It’s not a great experience for the audience and it’s key to moving forward, but you guys seem like you’re on it. So I won’t dwell on that.”

Nieman Lab requested a copy of the approved strategic plan but did not receive it by publication time. Read the full story in Current here.
